Fixed Deposit (FD): Types, Interest, Tax, Auto-Sweep and FD vs RD

A fixed deposit is a sum placed with a bank or NBFC for a set period at an agreed interest rate. This guide covers every type of FD, how the interest is worked out, how it is taxed, and how it compares with other choices.

3 min readFor MBA, BBA and BBMUpdated 2 November 2026

How an FD works

You deposit a lump sum for a period ranging from about 7 days to 10 years, at a rate fixed on that day. The rate stays the same until maturity, even if market rates change. At the end, you get your money back with interest. Banks may renew it automatically if you have asked them to.

Types of fixed deposit

TypeHow it worksGood for
Regular (standard) FDA fixed period at a fixed rateSafe saving for a known date
Cumulative FDInterest is reinvested and paid at maturityGrowing money
Non-cumulative FDInterest is paid monthly, quarterly or yearlyRegular income, such as for retirees
Senior citizen FDAn extra rate, often 0.25–0.75%, for those aged 60+Retirees
Tax-saving FDFive-year lock-in, with a deduction in the old tax regimeTax saving
Flexi or auto-sweep FDLinked to a savings account; money moves automaticallyEarning more on idle balance
Corporate FDPlaced with a company or NBFC, at a higher rate and with no DICGC coverThose comfortable with credit risk
Floating-rate FDThe rate moves with a benchmark such as the repo rateExpecting rates to rise
NRE, NRO and FCNR FDsFor non-residentsNRIs

Regular monthly saving is done through a recurring deposit, which is the natural partner of an FD. It has its own guide.

Auto-sweep explained

People often search for this as "auto swipe", but the banking term is auto-sweep or sweep-in. You set a limit on your savings account, such as ₹50,000. Anything above it moves into an FD automatically. If your balance falls short, money comes back from the FD, usually in small units, so most of the deposit keeps earning the FD rate.

  • Example: with a ₹50,000 limit and a ₹2,00,000 balance, ₹1,50,000 moves to an FD.
  • You get FD-level interest on idle money, while it remains available.
  • Interest is taxable, and early breaking may lower the rate on the part withdrawn. Check your bank's terms.

How FD interest is calculated

Maturity value = P × (1 + r/n)^(n × t). With ₹1,00,000 at 7% compounded quarterly for 5 years: 1,00,000 × (1 + 0.07/4)^20 = ₹1,41,478, so the interest is ₹41,478.

In a non-cumulative FD paying quarterly, the same deposit pays ₹1,750 a quarter, or ₹35,000 over 5 years. That is less in total, because the interest does not compound, but you get it as income along the way. Try the numbers in our FD calculator.

Tax and TDS

  • FD interest is added to your income and taxed at your slab rate, whether you receive it or it is reinvested.
  • Banks deduct TDS when interest crosses a yearly limit, currently ₹50,000 and ₹1 lakh for senior citizens, at 10% with PAN.
  • If your total income is below the taxable limit, you can submit Form 15G, or 15H for senior citizens, to avoid TDS, or claim the tax back when filing your ITR.
  • The tax-saving FD deduction is available only in the old regime, and interest on it is still taxable. Check the latest rules.

Is an FD safe?

  • Bank FDs are insured by DICGC up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, including interest.
  • Corporate FDs have no such cover, so check credit ratings from agencies such as CRISIL or ICRA.
  • Inflation is the hidden risk: at 7% interest, 30% tax and 5% inflation, the real return is about zero.

Laddering

Rather than putting everything in one FD, split the money across different maturities, such as 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 years. One FD matures each year, which provides regular liquidity and lowers the risk of locking everything in when rates are low.

Exam and interview questions

What are the types of fixed deposit?

Regular, cumulative, non-cumulative, senior citizen, tax-saving, flexi or auto-sweep, corporate, floating-rate, and NRE, NRO and FCNR deposits.

Can I break an FD early?

Yes, except for a tax-saving FD. You usually get the rate that applied for the shorter period, less a penalty that is often 0.5–1%.

What is the difference between an FD and an RD?

An FD takes one lump sum at the start. An RD takes a fixed amount every month. Each instalment in an RD earns interest only from when it is paid, so total interest is lower for the same total deposit.

What is auto-sweep in a bank account?

A facility that moves your balance above a set limit into an FD automatically, and brings it back when your account needs it. It is sometimes searched for as auto swipe.

Can I get a loan against an FD?

Yes. Banks usually lend up to about 90% of the FD value as a loan or overdraft, at a rate slightly above the FD rate, so you need not break it.
